problem: A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin $O$ with acceleration, measured in $\text{m}/{\text{s}}^{2},$ given by the function $a(t)=15-3t,$ where $t>0$ is the time in seconds. If the particle has velocity $v=14\,\text{m}/\text{s}$ when $t=1\,\text{s},$ calculate the maximum velocity ${v}_{\text{max}}$ of the particle and determine the time when the particle reaches its maximum velocity.

activity_context.topic_title: Determining Characteristics of Moving Objects Using Integration

examples.knowledge_point: Finding the Times at Which a Particle Reaches Its Maximum Velocity
examples.problem: A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin $O$ with acceleration, measured in $\textrm m / \textrm s^2,$ given by the function $a(t) = 6t-3t^2,$ where $t>0$ is the time in seconds. If the particle has velocity $v=2\,\textrm m / \textrm s$ when $t=1\,\textrm s,$ calculate the maximum velocity $v_{\text{max}}$ of the particle and determine the time when the particle reaches its maximum velocity.
examples.worked_solution:
The extrema of the velocity $v$ occur at the critical points of $v.$

Since $\dfrac{\textrm d v}{\textrm d t} = a(t),$ to find the times where $v$ is a maximum, we just need to solve $a(t) = 0$ and test each solution using the first or second derivative test.

Solving $a(t) = 0$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}a(t) & =0 \\ 6t-3{t}^{2} & =0 \\ 3t(2-t) & =0 \\ t & =0,\,2.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $t> 0$, the extremum of the velocity function occurs when $t = 2\,\textrm s.$

We now test the extreme value using the second derivative test. For this, we find the second derivative of $v(t)$ and evaluate it at $t=2\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}^{″}(t) & =\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}v}{\text{d}{t}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(a(t)) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(6t-3{t}^{2}) \\  & =6-6t \\ {v}^{″}(2) & =6-6(2) \\  & =-6\end{aligned}
$$

Since $v''(2) <      0,$ we conclude that the velocity is maximized when $t=2\,\textrm s.$

Now, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\text{d}t \\  & =\int (6t-3{t}^{2})\text{d}t \\  & =3{t}^{2}-{t}^{3}+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C$, we use the fact that $v(1) = 2.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}3(1)^{2}-(1)^{3}+C & =2 \\ 3-1+C & =2\,⟹\,C=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the velocity $v$ of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t) =3t^2-t^3.$

Finally, we calculate the maximum velocity:

$$
v_{\text{max}}= v(2) = 3(2)^2 - (2)^3 =4\,\textrm m / \textrm s
$$

So the maximum velocity $v_{\text{max}}=4\,\textrm m / \textrm s$ is reached at $t=2\,\textrm s.$

feedback.worked_solution:
First, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\text{d}t \\  & =\int (3{t}^{2}-2t-12)\text{d}t \\  & ={t}^{3}-{t}^{2}-12t+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C$, we use the fact that $v(4)=0.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}0 & =(4)^{3}-(4)^{2}-12(4)+C \\ 0 & =64-16-48+C \\ C & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the velocity $v$ of the runner at time $t$ is $v(t)={t}^{3}-{t}^{2}-12t.$

To find the time interval in which the runner is moving to the *left*, we must solve the inequality $v<0.$ This gives

$$
{t}^{3}-{t}^{2}-12t=t(t-4)(t+3)<0.
$$

Plotting the graph of $v(t)$, we get the following picture.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14063912/assets/27b9a41b0ad5c3ff98f6d76e24f0dc74e863d8f63a4c033fc41b7f7f2ebd72ea.png)

From the graph, we see that $v<0$ whenever $0\,<\,t\,<\,4.$
